title: Count enrolled students and groups by school
user_prompt: Using the students.csv and groups.csv files, how many students are currently enrolled in the program, and how many small-group sessions groups operate at each of the three schools?

gold_facts.claim: The program enrolls 135 students in total.
School SCH-001 has 60 enrolled students.
School SCH-002 has 45 enrolled students.
School SCH-003 has 30 enrolled students.
The program operates 14 tutoring groups across all three schools.
SCH-001 has 6 tutoring groups, SCH-002 has 5, and SCH-003 has 3.

gold_insights: The largest school by enrollment (SCH-001) also carries the most tutoring groups, while the smallest school (SCH-003) has fewer groups proportional to its size.
Eight students (about 5.9% of enrollees) have not yet been assigned to a tutoring group as of the reporting snapshot.
required_limitations: Student counts reflect enrollment as of the snapshot date; students who withdrew before that date are excluded.
Group counts describe the current active roster and do not reflect any mid-quarter reassignments.
forbidden_claims: All enrolled students have been assigned to a tutoring group.
The program operates more than 14 or fewer than 14 groups.
Enrollment figures reflect academic-year cumulative counts.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: Every numeric count must exactly match the rows in students.csv and groups.csv.

insight_quality.guidance: Answer should note the school-size distribution and the unassigned-student gap.

evidence_linkage.guidance: School-level counts must cite the school_id column in students.csv and groups.csv.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Model must not over-generalise beyond the snapshot date.

reference_answer_outline: Report total enrollment (135) broken down by school (60/45/30). Report 14 groups broken down by school (6/5/3). Note 8 students lack a group assignment. Caveat that all figures are point-in-time snapshots.

title: Compute program-wide session attendance rate for the full reporting quarter
user_prompt: Using sessions.csv and attendance.csv, what is the overall student attendance rate across all completed sessions for the full September–November 2025 reporting quarter? Express the result as a percentage rounded to one decimal place.

gold_facts.claim: There are 457 completed sessions across the full quarter.
Across all completed sessions, there are 4156 student-attendance records.
3363 of those 4156 student-attendance records show the student attended.
The program-wide student attendance rate for the quarter is approximately 80.9% (0.8092).

gold_insights: The program's 80.9% quarterly attendance rate narrowly clears the stated goal of 80%, indicating the program is on track but has limited margin.
Computing attendance rate only over completed sessions avoids inflating or deflating the rate by cancelled or no-show sessions.
required_limitations: Attendance is recorded at the student-session level; a student present for part of a session is counted as attended if the tutor recorded the student as present.
Cancelled sessions are excluded from the attendance denominator; including them would substantially lower the computed rate.
forbidden_claims: The attendance rate is computed by dividing completed sessions by total scheduled sessions.
The attendance rate exceeds 85% for the quarter.
All 135 enrolled students have equal numbers of attendance records.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: The 80.9% rate must be derived correctly: attended rows / total rows for completed sessions only.

insight_quality.guidance: Should note proximity to the 80% goal without fabricating causal claims.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Must cite both sessions.csv (to filter to completed) and attendance.csv (for the attended flag).

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must clarify that cancelled sessions are excluded from the denominator.

reference_answer_outline: Step 1: filter sessions.csv to status='completed' (457 sessions). Step 2: join attendance.csv on session_id to get 4156 records. Step 3: count attended=true rows (3363). Step 4: 3363/4156 = 80.9%. Note the goal is 80% and the program is just above it. Mention cancellation exclusion caveat.

title: Retrieve and compare monthly attendance rates across the quarter
user_prompt: Using sessions.csv and attendance.csv, what was the student attendance rate for each month of the reporting period (September, October, and November 2025)? Which month had the lowest rate, and by how many percentage points did it differ from the highest month?

gold_facts.claim: The September 2025 attendance rate across completed sessions is approximately 78.8% (0.7879).
The October 2025 attendance rate across completed sessions is approximately 82.4% (0.8236).
The November 2025 attendance rate across completed sessions is approximately 82.0% (0.8196).
September had the lowest monthly attendance rate (78.8%), and October had the highest (82.4%), a difference of approximately 3.6 percentage points.

gold_insights: Despite October having the highest session-level cancellation rate of the quarter, students who did attend completed sessions in October had a higher attendance rate than in September, suggesting that students with better commitment patterns were the ones attending amid disruptions.
The attendance rate improved from September to October and remained nearly flat through November, indicating a stabilising trend after the program launch.
required_limitations: Monthly rates are computed only over completed sessions; months with more cancellations have fewer sessions in the denominator.
September figures may reflect lower engagement typical of a program launch month rather than a true structural attendance problem.
forbidden_claims: October had the lowest attendance rate.
The attendance rate declined every month across the quarter.
The difference between highest and lowest monthly rates exceeds 10 percentage points.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: All three monthly rates must match the fixture data to within 0.1 pp.

insight_quality.guidance: A strong answer connects October cancellation rate with October attendance rate, noting they measure different things.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Each rate must be attributed to the correct month from sessions.csv.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must note that cancellation exclusion affects comparability across months.

reference_answer_outline: Filter sessions by month, join attendance, compute attended/total per month: Sep=78.8%, Oct=82.4%, Nov=82.0%. September is lowest, October is highest, gap=3.6 pp. Note September launch-month caveat and October cancellation exclusion.

title: Identify and quantify the October cancellation spike
user_prompt: Using sessions.csv, what was the session cancellation rate in October 2025 — counting sessions that were cancelled (by any party) or resulted in a no-show, out of all scheduled sessions — and how does it compare to September and November? Provide the rate for all three months and the absolute difference (in percentage points) between October and the average of the other two months.

gold_facts.claim: The September 2025 cancellation rate is approximately 10.6% (20 of 188 scheduled sessions were cancelled or no-shows).
The October 2025 cancellation rate is approximately 27.9% (53 of 190 scheduled sessions were cancelled or no-shows).
The November 2025 cancellation rate is approximately 9.5% (16 of 168 scheduled sessions were cancelled or no-shows).
October's cancellation rate (27.9%) is approximately 17.8 percentage points above the average of September and November (10.1%).

gold_insights: October's cancellation rate of 27.9% is roughly 2.8 times the ~10% average of the surrounding months, representing a clear operational disruption rather than typical variance.

Of the 53 October sessions that did not occur, 40 were cancellations (19 student-initiated, 14 tutor-initiated, 7 school-initiated) and 13 were no-shows, suggesting multiple concurrent causes rather than a single root cause.
required_limitations: The cancellation rate is computed as (cancelled + no-show) sessions / all scheduled sessions; it does not account for whether sessions were later rescheduled.
The cancellation categories (cancelled_school, cancelled_student, cancelled_tutor) are self-reported by the recording party and may be inconsistently applied.
forbidden_claims: The October cancellation rate was caused solely by school schedule conflicts.
November had a higher cancellation rate than September.
The overall quarterly cancellation rate exceeded 30%.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: All three monthly cancellation rates and the arithmetic comparison must match fixture data.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers break October's non-occurring sessions into cancellations (by type) and no-shows using the status column.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Must cite specific session counts from sessions.csv.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must note that cancellation type labels are self-reported and rescheduling is unknown.

reference_answer_outline: Count scheduled sessions per month (Sep=188, Oct=190, Nov=168). Count cancelled-or-no-show (Sep=20, Oct=53, Nov=16). Rates: Sep=10.6%, Oct=27.9%, Nov=9.5%. Oct vs avg(Sep,Nov)=10.1%: difference=17.8 pp. Break October's 53 into 40 cancellations (by type) + 13 no-shows. Note rescheduling unknown caveat.

title: Compute the IEP versus non-IEP attendance gap
user_prompt: Using students.csv, sessions.csv, and attendance.csv, compute the student attendance rate separately for students with an Individualized Education Program (IEP) designation and for those without. What is the gap in percentage points between the two groups?

gold_facts.claim: There are 15 students with an IEP designation and 120 students without.
The attendance rate for students with an IEP designation across completed sessions is approximately 68.4% (305 attended out of 446 records).
The attendance rate for students without an IEP designation across completed sessions is approximately 82.4% (3058 attended out of 3710 records).
The gap between non-IEP and IEP attendance rates is approximately 14.0 percentage points.

gold_insights: The 14-percentage-point gap between IEP and non-IEP attendance substantially exceeds the program's stated goal of reducing the gap to 5 percentage points or fewer, signalling a priority area for targeted outreach.
IEP students constitute 11% of enrollment but account for a disproportionate share of absences relative to their group size.
required_limitations: IEP status is a binary flag as recorded in students.csv; it does not capture the type or severity of the students' needs, which may affect attendance patterns differently.
The IEP subgroup is small (15 students), so individual absences by even one or two students can materially shift the computed rate; this figure should be interpreted with caution.
This analysis does not control for school or grade-level effects that may be correlated with IEP status in this cohort.
forbidden_claims: IEP students have the same attendance rate as non-IEP students.
The IEP attendance gap has been closing over the quarter.
The gap exceeds 20 percentage points.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: Both subgroup rates and the gap must match the fixture data to within 0.2 pp.

insight_quality.guidance: Should benchmark the gap against the stated program goal of ≤5 pp.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Must show the join logic across all three source files.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Small IEP-group caveat and lack of confound controls must be acknowledged.

reference_answer_outline: Join students.csv (iep flag) → attendance.csv → sessions.csv (filter completed). IEP: 305/446 = 68.4%. Non-IEP: 3058/3710 = 82.4%. Gap = 14.0 pp. Note goal is ≤5 pp, group is small (n=15), and confounders not controlled.

title: Retrieve November 2025 session and attendance metrics as the most-recent complete month
user_prompt: The program director asks for a summary of last month's activity. Assuming the current reporting date is December 1, 2025, use sessions.csv and attendance.csv to report: (a) the total number of sessions scheduled and completed in November 2025, (b) the student attendance rate for completed November sessions, and (c) how November's attendance rate compares to the overall quarter rate.

gold_facts.claim: 168 sessions were scheduled in November 2025.
152 of the 168 November sessions were completed, giving a session completion rate of approximately 90.5%.
The student attendance rate for completed November 2025 sessions is approximately 82.0% (1136 attended out of 1386 attendance records).
November's 82.0% attendance rate is approximately 1.0 percentage point above the full-quarter rate of 80.9%.

gold_insights: November is the strongest attendance month of the quarter, and the program ended the reporting period on an improving trajectory relative to its 80% goal.
Session completion also improved in November: 90.5% of scheduled sessions were completed, compared to 72.1% in October, indicating recovery from the October disruption.
required_limitations: Interpreting November as 'last month' depends on the assumed reporting date; if the reporting date were different, a different month would be current.
A single month's attendance figure may be influenced by end-of-quarter effects such as increased engagement before a break period; it should not be projected forward without additional data.
forbidden_claims: November had the highest cancellation rate of the quarter.
November attendance was below the 80% program goal.
The program completed all 168 scheduled November sessions.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: November scheduled count (168), completed count (152), attendance rate (82.0%), and quarter comparison must all match fixtures.

insight_quality.guidance: Strong answers contextualise November as a recovery month after October's cancellation spike.

evidence_linkage.guidance: Must filter sessions by date range and cite program_context.json for the reporting-period anchor.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must acknowledge the relative-time interpretation and single-month projection caveat.

reference_answer_outline: Interpret 'last month' as November 2025 given Dec 1 reporting date. sessions.csv: Nov total=168, completed=152. attendance.csv (Nov completed sessions): 1136/1386 = 82.0%. Quarter rate = 80.9%. Gap = +1.0 pp. Note Oct recovery context and single-month caveat.

title: Identify the highest-priority tutor for operational coaching based on attendance metrics
user_prompt: Using tutors.csv, groups.csv, sessions.csv, and attendance.csv for the September–November 2025 quarter, identify which tutor should be the top coaching priority based on student attendance outcomes. Rank all tutors by their student attendance rate across completed sessions, identify the lowest-performing tutor, and recommend two specific operational actions to address the attendance gap. Cite the tutor ID, group IDs, and numeric attendance rates that support your recommendation.

gold_facts.claim: TUT-005 (SCH-002, paraprofessional) has the lowest student attendance rate among all tutors at approximately 76.4% (440 attended out of 576 records across completed sessions in GRP-007 and GRP-010).
TUT-005's attendance rate of 76.4% is approximately 4.5 percentage points below the program-wide rate of 80.9%.
TUT-005 leads two groups: GRP-007 (math, grade 3, SCH-002, attendance 73.96%) and GRP-010 (reading, grade 6, SCH-002, attendance 78.82%). GRP-007 is the lowest-attending group in the program.
The program-wide student attendance rate across all completed sessions is approximately 80.9% (3363 attended out of 4156 records).

gold_insights: TUT-005 should be the top coaching priority because both of their groups fall below the 80% program goal, with GRP-007 at 73.96% being the single lowest-attending group program-wide.

Targeted outreach to consistently absent students in GRP-007 (grade 3 math at SCH-002) combined with a session-structure review for TUT-005 could address the attendance gap; however, correlation between tutor practice and attendance should be verified before attributing the gap solely to instructional delivery.
Raising TUT-005's attendance rate by 4.5 percentage points would contribute meaningfully to meeting the program-wide 80% goal.
required_limitations: Attendance rates are computed at the student-session level across completed sessions only; cancelled or no-show sessions are excluded from the denominator.

Low attendance in a tutor's groups may reflect student-side factors (e.g., transportation, family schedule) rather than instructional quality; further qualitative investigation is required before attributing the gap to the tutor.
This ranking uses a single metric (student attendance rate); a holistic coaching priority decision would also consider session rating data, IEP subgroup outcomes, and cancellation patterns.
forbidden_claims: TUT-005's attendance rate is below 70%.
GRP-007 has an attendance rate above 80%.
Low attendance is definitively caused by the tutor's instructional approach.
TUT-005 is the only tutor below the 80% program goal.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: TUT-005's rate (76.4%), GRP-007's rate (73.96%), GRP-010's rate (78.82%), and the program-wide rate (80.9%) must all be cited and match the fixture data within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Recommendations must be specific and actionable (e.g., target GRP-007 students for outreach, review session structure), not generic coaching advice. Must connect group-level rates to the program goal.

evidence_linkage.guidance: REQUIRED: Recommendations must explicitly cite TUT-005, GRP-007, GRP-010, and the numeric attendance rates from sessions.csv and attendance.csv as the evidentiary basis. Generic recommendations without data citations receive zero credit on this dimension.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must acknowledge that attendance gaps may reflect student-side factors and that a single metric ranking is incomplete for holistic coaching decisions.

structure_usability.guidance: Should present tutor ranking clearly and separate the diagnostic finding from the actionable recommendations.

reference_answer_outline: Rank all 9 tutors by attendance rate. TUT-005 is lowest at 76.4% (GRP-007: 73.96%, GRP-010: 78.82%). Program-wide rate: 80.9%; gap = 4.5 pp. Recommend: (1) targeted attendance outreach for chronically absent students in GRP-007; (2) observational coaching visit for TUT-005 to diagnose structural session barriers. Caveat: student-side factors, single-metric limitation.

title: Prioritize tutors for IEP student support based on subgroup attendance data
user_prompt: Using students.csv, groups.csv, sessions.csv, and attendance.csv, analyze the attendance rate of students with an IEP designation disaggregated by the tutor leading their group. Identify which tutors serve IEP students and which should be prioritized for coaching support to close the IEP attendance gap. Cite specific tutor IDs, group IDs, and numeric IEP attendance rates in your recommendations.

gold_facts.claim: The program-wide IEP student attendance rate is approximately 68.4% (305 attended out of 446 records across completed sessions).
TUT-005 (SCH-002) has the lowest IEP student attendance rate among tutors with IEP students: approximately 62.5% (100 attended out of 160 IEP student-session records across GRP-007 and GRP-010).

TUT-008 (SCH-003) has an IEP student attendance rate of approximately 57.6% in GRP-012 (19 attended out of 33 IEP student-session records), the lowest IEP attendance rate of any single group with IEP students.
The non-IEP student attendance rate is approximately 82.4%, creating an IEP attendance gap of approximately 14.0 percentage points program-wide.

gold_insights: TUT-005 and TUT-008 should be the top two coaching priorities for IEP student support: TUT-005 serves the largest volume of IEP student-session records (160) at 62.5%, while TUT-008's GRP-012 at SCH-003 has the lowest single-group IEP rate at 57.6%.

The 14.0 percentage-point IEP attendance gap substantially exceeds the program's stated goal of reducing the gap to 5 percentage points or fewer, indicating a systemic rather than isolated issue requiring coordinated intervention.
Not all tutors have IEP students in their groups; coaching should be directed specifically at TUT-005 (GRP-007, GRP-010) and TUT-008 (GRP-012), where the evidentiary need is greatest.
required_limitations: IEP student subgroups within individual tutor-led groups are small (n=1 to 4 students in most groups); rates in small groups can shift substantially with one or two additional absences and should be interpreted with caution.
This analysis does not control for school-level, grade-level, or subject-area confounders that may be correlated with both IEP designation and attendance patterns.
IEP status is a binary flag; the type and severity of individual students' needs vary and may affect attendance differently than the binary classification suggests.
forbidden_claims: The IEP attendance gap has been closing over the quarter.
All tutors with IEP students have similar IEP attendance rates.
The IEP attendance gap exceeds 20 percentage points.
TUT-008 serves no IEP students.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: Program-wide IEP rate (68.4%), TUT-005 IEP rate (62.5%), TUT-008 GRP-012 IEP rate (57.6%), and the 14.0 pp gap must all be cited and match fixture data.

insight_quality.guidance: Must identify TUT-005 and TUT-008 as top priorities with distinct rationale for each (volume vs. lowest group rate). Must connect findings to the program's stated 5 pp IEP gap goal.

evidence_linkage.guidance: REQUIRED: Coaching recommendations must explicitly cite tutor IDs (TUT-005, TUT-008), group IDs (GRP-007, GRP-010, GRP-012), and the numeric IEP attendance rates from the fixture data. A recommendation that does not name specific tutors, groups, and rates from the data earns zero on this dimension.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must acknowledge small IEP subgroup sizes within individual groups and absence of confound controls.

structure_usability.guidance: Present a clear priority ordering with supporting evidence for each priority.

reference_answer_outline: Program-wide IEP rate: 68.4%, non-IEP: 82.4%, gap: 14.0 pp (vs. goal of <=5 pp). Tutors with IEP students: TUT-001 (74.2%), TUT-002 (68.75%), TUT-004 (76.7%), TUT-005 (62.5%), TUT-006 (73.5%), TUT-008 (57.6% in GRP-012). Top priorities: (1) TUT-005 - largest IEP volume at lowest rate; (2) TUT-008 GRP-012 - lowest single-group IEP rate. Note small-n caveat and confounders.

title: Recommend operational actions to address the October cancellation spike and prevent recurrence
user_prompt: Using sessions.csv and program_context.json, analyze the October 2025 session cancellation pattern by tutor and recommend the top two operational actions to prevent a similar disruption in the next quarter. Cite the specific monthly cancellation rates, the tutors with the highest cancellation exposure in October, and the session-status breakdown that supports your recommendations.

gold_facts.claim: The October 2025 cancellation rate (cancelled + no-show sessions out of all scheduled October sessions) is approximately 27.9% (53 out of 190 scheduled sessions).

TUT-004 (SCH-001) has the highest quarterly cancellation rate among all tutors at approximately 23.1% (9 cancelled/no-show out of 39 sessions), and in October specifically had 5 of 13 sessions (38.5%) cancelled or no-show.

The September 2025 cancellation rate was approximately 10.6% and the November 2025 rate was approximately 9.5%, making October's rate approximately 17.8 percentage points above the average of the surrounding months.
TUT-008 (SCH-003) has the second-highest quarterly cancellation rate at approximately 20.5% (16 of 78 sessions).

gold_insights: The October spike at 27.9% is nearly three times the surrounding months' average of ~10%, suggesting a systemic scheduling conflict or external disruption rather than random variance; a root-cause investigation targeting October-specific events is warranted before next quarter.

TUT-004's October cancellation rate of 38.5% is the most acute individual exposure and warrants a direct follow-up conversation; however, the program-wide spike indicates the cause is not isolated to one tutor.

Two specific operational actions: (1) establish a shared quarterly calendar with all three schools before the next quarter starts to flag known conflict dates; (2) implement a mid-month check-in with tutors who exceed 20% cancellation rate in any rolling 4-week window to identify and resolve barriers earlier.
required_limitations: The cancellation-type labels (cancelled_student, cancelled_tutor, cancelled_school, no_show) are self-reported by the recording party and may be inconsistently applied across sites.
This analysis cannot determine whether cancelled sessions were later rescheduled; the true instructional time lost may be lower than raw cancellation counts suggest.
The October spike may reflect a one-time external event and may not be predictive of future quarters without additional context from school administrators.
forbidden_claims: The October cancellation spike was definitively caused by a single tutor.
November had a higher cancellation rate than October.
All cancelled sessions result in permanent instructional time loss.
The overall quarterly cancellation rate exceeded 30%.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: October rate (27.9%), September rate (10.6%), November rate (9.5%), TUT-004 quarterly rate (23.1%), and TUT-008 rate (20.5%) must all match fixture data within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Recommendations must be specific and preventive (not reactive), grounded in the pattern observed. Should distinguish individual-tutor issues from program-wide systemic causes.

evidence_linkage.guidance: REQUIRED: Each operational recommendation must be explicitly tied to specific evidence from the fixture data, citing at minimum: the monthly cancellation rates (sessions.csv), the specific tutor IDs with highest cancellation exposure (TUT-004, TUT-008), and the numerical gap between October and surrounding months. Recommendations that do not cite specific fixture-derived evidence earn zero on this dimension.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must acknowledge self-reporting bias in cancellation-type labels and uncertainty about rescheduling.

structure_usability.guidance: Clearly separate the diagnostic analysis from the two recommended actions.

reference_answer_outline: Oct cancel rate: 27.9% (53/190). Sep: 10.6%, Nov: 9.5%. Oct above average by 17.8 pp. Tutor breakdown: TUT-004 highest at 23.1% quarterly / 38.5% in October; TUT-008 at 20.5% quarterly. Actions: (1) shared school calendar alignment before Q2; (2) rolling 4-week tutor check-in trigger at >20% cancel rate. Caveats: self-reported labels, rescheduling unknown.

title: Confidence-banded recommendation for school-level attendance intervention
user_prompt: Using groups.csv, sessions.csv, and attendance.csv, compute the student attendance rate at each of the three schools for the full September–November 2025 quarter. Produce a confidence-banded recommendation: for each school, assign a confidence level (high / medium / low) to your intervention recommendation based on the strength of the evidence, and cite the specific attendance rates and sample sizes that justify each confidence band.

gold_facts.claim: SCH-001 has the highest school-level student attendance rate at approximately 82.5% (1456 attended out of 1765 records across completed sessions).
SCH-002 has the lowest school-level student attendance rate at approximately 78.9% (1121 attended out of 1421 records across completed sessions), below the 80% program goal.
SCH-003 has a student attendance rate of approximately 81.0% (786 attended out of 970 records across completed sessions), meeting the 80% program goal.
SCH-002's attendance rate of 78.9% is approximately 3.6 percentage points below SCH-001's rate of 82.5%, and approximately 1.1 percentage points below the 80% program goal.

gold_insights: SCH-002 should receive a high-confidence recommendation for attendance intervention: its 78.9% rate is the only school-level rate below the 80% program goal, is supported by 1421 attendance records (the second-largest sample), and the gap of ~1.1 pp below goal is small enough that a targeted action could close it within a quarter.

SCH-001 and SCH-003 both meet the 80% goal; a medium-confidence maintenance recommendation is appropriate for SCH-003 (smaller sample, 970 records) and a low-urgency monitoring recommendation for SCH-001 (strongest performer at 82.5% with the largest sample of 1765 records).
The confidence banding should reflect both statistical stability (larger samples yield more reliable rates) and proximity to the intervention threshold (80% goal), not just the point estimate alone.
required_limitations: School-level rates aggregate across all tutors and groups within each school; a school below goal may contain a mix of high- and low-performing groups, and a school-wide intervention may miss root causes concentrated in specific groups.

The three schools differ in enrollment (60, 45, and 30 students at SCH-001, SCH-002, and SCH-003 respectively), which affects the statistical reliability of school-level rates; the smallest school's rate should be interpreted with greater caution.
These rates reflect one quarter of data; a single quarter is insufficient to distinguish a structural attendance pattern from a temporary fluctuation.
forbidden_claims: SCH-002's attendance rate exceeds 80%.
All three schools have the same attendance rate.
SCH-003 is below the 80% program goal.
The school-level difference between SCH-001 and SCH-002 exceeds 10 percentage points.

grounding_accuracy.guidance: SCH-001 (82.5%), SCH-002 (78.9%), and SCH-003 (81.0%) rates and their sample sizes must match fixture data within tolerance.

insight_quality.guidance: Confidence banding must be explicitly justified by citing both the numeric attendance rate and the sample size for each school. Generic confidence bands without numeric support should be penalized.

evidence_linkage.guidance: REQUIRED: Each school's confidence-band assignment and its associated recommendation must cite the school ID, the numeric attendance rate, the number of attendance records used, and their relationship to the 80% program goal from the fixture data. Confidence bands assigned without explicit fixture-grounded evidence earn zero on this dimension.

calibration_limitation_handling.guidance: Must acknowledge that school-level aggregation may mask within-school variation and that one quarter of data is insufficient for trend inference.

structure_usability.guidance: Should present a clear table or structured list: school, rate, sample size, confidence band, recommendation.

reference_answer_outline: Compute school attendance: SCH-001=82.5% (n=1765), SCH-002=78.9% (n=1421), SCH-003=81.0% (n=970). SCH-002 below 80% goal by 1.1 pp — HIGH confidence intervention. SCH-003 above goal but smallest sample — MEDIUM confidence maintenance. SCH-001 highest rate, largest sample — LOW urgency monitoring. Confidence justified by proximity to goal AND sample size. Caveat: within-school variation, single-quarter data.

title: Synthesize multi-signal coaching priority list integrating attendance, cancellation, and session-volume evidence
user_prompt: Using tutors.csv, groups.csv, sessions.csv, and attendance.csv, produce a ranked coaching priority list for all nine tutors integrating three signals: (1) student attendance rate, (2) session cancellation rate, and (3) sessions delivered year-to-date. For the top two priority tutors, provide specific coaching recommendations with cited evidence. Acknowledge uncertainty where signals conflict or data is missing.

gold_facts.claim: TUT-005 (SCH-002, paraprofessional) has the lowest student attendance rate at 76.4% (440/576) and the joint-highest session count year-to-date (78 sessions), representing both the most systemic attendance concern and the highest workload exposure.

TUT-004 (SCH-001, paraprofessional) has the highest session cancellation rate at 23.1% (9 of 39 sessions cancelled or no-show) but a student attendance rate of 81.9% (221/270) for sessions that did occur, meaning the sessions that complete are high-quality in attendance terms.

TUT-002 (SCH-001, paraprofessional) and TUT-008 (SCH-003, paraprofessional) both have the lowest sessions-delivered year-to-date count of 35 sessions each, indicating substantially lower instructional dosage than the highest-volume tutors at 78 sessions.
TUT-003 (SCH-001, certified_teacher) has the highest student attendance rate at 85.5% (282/330) among all tutors and is the only tutor without a session rating on record.

gold_insights: TUT-005 is the top coaching priority based on multi-signal evidence: lowest attendance rate (76.4%), high workload (78 sessions YTD), and two groups both below the 80% threshold — the combination of scale and underperformance creates the greatest aggregate impact on the program.

TUT-004 is the second priority for a different reason: the high cancellation rate (23.1%) suggests scheduling or commitment barriers that, if unaddressed, risk compounding in a future quarter despite the adequate attendance rate in sessions that do occur; coaching should focus on proactive scheduling rather than instructional delivery.

TUT-003 and TUT-009 have missing session rating data, which creates a gap in the multi-signal picture; for these tutors, the missing data itself warrants follow-up to ensure the data collection system is functioning correctly before a full coaching assessment can be made.
required_limitations: Session ratings in tutors.csv are self-reported averages and may reflect self-report bias; they should be treated as one corroborating signal, not a definitive quality measure.
Year-to-date session counts in tutors.csv are as-of the snapshot date and may not accurately capture all sessions if data entry was delayed.
Signals were combined qualitatively here; a formal composite score would require explicitly defined weights and would still encode subjective priority choices.
TUT-003 and TUT-009 have no avg_session_rating data recorded; their multi-signal profiles are incomplete and conclusions about them carry additional uncertainty.
forbidden_claims: TUT-003 has a session rating on record.
TUT-005 has the highest cancellation rate.
TUT-009 has the highest year-to-date session count.
TUT-004's attendance rate is below the 80% program goal.
